steps.text: Part 4 of 4: Check, checkmate or neither?. This part covers Check yourself. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

Dan Heisman, a chess coach, advises listing the opponent's checks, captures and threats before you move (chess.com article, secondary source). [I] Running the four questions on each check you find is one way to use that. [H] Practising on positions you did not set up may make it quick; no study here tests that.

steps.prompt: Explain to a friend why a queen next to the king is sometimes checkmate and sometimes not. Say it aloud or write it down, then compare with the model answer next.

steps.text: **Model answer.** First ask whether the king is attacked; if not, it is neither. If it is, ask: can I take the checker, put something in the way, or move the king to a safe square? Any yes means only check. A queen beside the king is mate only if something guards her, so the king cannot take her, and every other square is covered. Three closed doors, and the king attacked, mean checkmate. Knight and pawn checks cannot be blocked.
